title: Question 2: Housing and Homeownership ($120 million)

context.text: Placed on the ballot by the General Assembly: the Rhode Island Voter Information Handbook describes Questions 1 through 5 as authorizing the State to borrow through bonds and temporary notes for capital investments under an act passed at the January 2026 session (Chapter 084, Public Laws 2026).

question.text: Shall the act passed by the General Assembly at the January 2026 session, allowing the State of Rhode Island to issue bonds, refunding bonds, and temporary notes to pay for the projects listed below, be approved, and the State be allowed to issue these bonds, refunding bonds, and temporary notes as outlined in the law? 2. HOUSING AND HOMEOWNERSHIP - $120,000,000 To increase and preserve the availability of affordable and accessible housing to meet the needs of all Rhode Islanders and support community revitalization through the redevelopment of existing structures, new construction, property acquisition, and infrastructure improvements. Of this amount, at least twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000) shall be allocated towards increasing production of housing intended for homeownership and up to ten million dollars ($10,000,000) may be used to support a program for public housing development.

summary.text: The bond would provide $120,000,000 to increase housing availability and supply, revitalize communities and promote affordable homeownership, through new construction and renovation of existing buildings. At least $25,000,000 must go toward housing intended for homeownership and up to $10,000,000 may support a public housing development program. Official cost estimate in the handbook (assuming 5% interest and level payments over 20 years): principal $120,000,000, interest $72,586,000, total $192,586,000.

measure.yesMeans: A vote to Approve means that you support the State issuing $120,000,000 in general obligation bonds to increase housing and homeownership.
measure.noMeans: A vote to Reject means that you are against the State issuing $120,000,000 in general obligation bonds to increase housing and homeownership.

fiscalImpact.text: Per the Rhode Island Department of State handbook: $120,000,000 in general obligation bonds. Assuming 5% interest and level payments over 20 years, interest is $72,586,000 and total cost $192,586,000 (cost of issuance estimated at 0.4% of principal). Housing projects are expected to begin by 2028 and be completed between 2029 and 2032; estimated useful life is a minimum of 30 years.

supporters.text: Yes on 2 campaign, which describes itself as a broad-based coalition of individuals, organizations and community leaders.
Housing Network of Rhode Island (Executive Director Melina Lodge), in testimony supporting Question 2 while urging a larger $150 million bond.
One Neighborhood Builders (Peter Chapman), in testimony supporting Question 2 while urging a larger $150 million bond.

researchNotes: The ballot text, approve/reject statements and cost estimates are from the Rhode Island Department of State's 2026 Voter Information Handbook (PDF text extracted and checked by script). The handbook publishes no arguments for or against, and no verbatim argument against the measure was found; the argument lists are left empty so both sides stay balanced (supporters, where found, are listed under supporters). Coverage found (Rhode Island Current) discusses results of the 2024 housing bond rather than Question 2, so it is not used. The Secretary of State's website and Ballotpedia blocked automated requests; the five-question list is from the handbook, which covers all statewide referenda. Added (Oct. 19): full text is Article 5 of H 7127 Sub A as amended (enacted as Public Laws 2026 ch. 84); cost figures restate the handbook. No campaign-finance totals were found (the state campaign-finance portal was not queried). Supporters: the Yes on 2 campaign's own site and two February 2026 House Finance Committee letters. A campaign launch release reposted by a partisan blog was removed as a source and its details (spokesperson, funders) are not used; the original release could not be found. No named organized opposition was found (RIPEC criticized how the 2024 bond has performed, per Rhode Island Current, but did not take a position on Question 2).
